name: gcc
summary: The GNU C compiler: compile, link, show warnings, and produce debug builds.

install.note: Cross compilers have prefixed names such as aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc (Debian package gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu). In Yocto, source the SDK environment script and use $CC instead, which includes the right sysroot flags.

compat: clang accepts most of the same options. A program compiled for your PC (x86_64) will not run on an ARM board, and vice versa: check with file.

examples.title: Compile and link one C file with warnings and debug info
examples.explain: Produces the executable <output>; run it with ./<output>. Always read warnings: they often point at real bugs.
examples.warning: Overwrites <output> if it already exists; never use your source file's name as <output>.
options: Name of the output file (default a.out)
examples.output: No output means success. 'undefined reference to ...' is a link error (missing .c file or -l library); 'No such file or directory' for a header means its -dev/-devel package or -I path is missing.

examples.title: Compile to an object file only
examples.explain: -c stops before linking. Larger programs compile each .c to .o and link them together in a final step.

examples.title: Link with a library and add a header search path
examples.explain: -I adds a directory searched for #include files. -lm links libm.so (math), -lpthread pthreads, etc. Put -l options after the source files.

examples.title: See the preprocessed source
examples.explain: Shows what the compiler really sees after #include and #define are expanded; useful for macro puzzles.

examples.title: Show which version and target you are compiling for
examples.explain: The 'Target:' line (e.g. x86_64-linux-gnu or aarch64-linux-gnu) tells you which architecture the binaries will be for.

name: make
summary: Build programs from a Makefile, rebuilding only what changed.
compat: Recipe lines in a Makefile must start with a real Tab, not spaces; otherwise you get 'missing separator'. Check with cat -A Makefile (tabs show as ^I).

examples.title: Build the default target
examples.explain: Runs the first target in ./Makefile. It prints each command before running it.
examples.output: 'Nothing to be done' / 'is up to date' means outputs are newer than their inputs. 'No targets specified and no makefile found' means you are in the wrong directory.

examples.title: Build in another directory
examples.explain: Kernel modules are built this way: make -C /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build M=$PWD modules (needs the kernel headers package).

examples.title: Show what would run without running it
examples.explain: Dry run: an inspect-first way to understand an unfamiliar Makefile, including what clean or install would do.

examples.title: Parallel build using all CPU cores
examples.explain: Runs independent steps at the same time. If the output is confusing, rerun without -j to see errors in order.

examples.title: Remove build outputs
examples.explain: Runs the Makefile's clean target. What it deletes is defined by the Makefile author, so check with make -n clean first in unfamiliar projects.
examples.warning: Deletes whatever the clean recipe says. Inspect it first with make -n clean.

name: cmake
summary: Generate and run builds for projects that use CMakeLists.txt.
compat: -S/-B need CMake 3.13+ and --build needs 3.15+ for -j. For cross-compiling pass -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=<file>; the Yocto SDK provides one via its environment script.

examples.title: Configure into a separate build directory
examples.explain: Run in the directory with CMakeLists.txt. Keeping generated files in build/ means you can delete that folder to start fresh.
examples.output: Ends with 'Build files have been written to'. 'Could NOT find <Package>' means a development package is missing.

examples.title: Build
examples.explain: Calls the underlying tool (make or ninja) for you.

name: gdb
summary: The GNU debugger: run a program step by step, inspect variables, and see where it crashed.

install.note: For a board, run gdbserver on the target and gdb-multiarch (or the SDK's gdb) on your PC.

compat: Compile with -g (and ideally -O0) for readable debugging.

examples.title: Start a program under the debugger
examples.explain: Inside gdb: break main, run, next (n), step (s), print <var> (p), bt for a backtrace, quit (q).
options: Everything after the program name is passed to it as arguments

examples.title: Get a backtrace from a crash, non-interactively
examples.explain: Runs the program; if it crashes (e.g. SIGSEGV), prints the call stack showing the function and line.
examples.output: Frame #0 is where it crashed; higher frames are the callers. '??' means no debug info: rebuild with -g.

name: strace
summary: Trace the system calls a program makes: which files it opens, what fails, and why.
compat: Tracing processes you do not own (or attaching with -p) may need root or a relaxed kernel.yama.ptrace_scope.

examples.title: See which files a program tries to open
examples.explain: Great for 'file not found' mysteries: look for = -1 ENOENT next to the path it expected.
options: Also trace child processes and threads
examples.output: Each line is call(args) = result. A negative result with a name like EACCES or ENOENT is the error the program got.

examples.title: Trace device access to a character device
examples.explain: When testing your own driver from user space, this shows exactly which calls reached it and their return values.
options: Comma-separated list of syscalls to show

examples.title: Summary of syscall counts and errors
examples.explain: Prints a table after the program exits: which calls were made, how often, and how many failed.
options: Count calls and print a summary

name: readelf
summary: Show ELF file details: architecture, sections, symbols and needed libraries.
compat: readelf works on ELF files for any architecture, so it can inspect ARM binaries on an x86 PC (unlike objdump, which may need a multiarch build).

examples.title: Show the ELF header
examples.explain: Machine shows the target CPU; Type is EXEC/DYN (program or shared object) or REL (object file or .ko kernel module).

examples.title: Which shared libraries does it need?
examples.explain: Safe alternative to ldd for untrusted binaries: it only reads the file.

examples.title: List sections
examples.explain: Shows .text (code), .data, .bss, .rodata and their sizes; in a .ko, .modinfo holds module metadata.

name: objdump
summary: Disassemble machine code and display object file contents.

install.note: For other architectures use the cross version, e.g. aarch64-linux-gnu-objdump.

compat: Use the objdump matching the binary's architecture.

examples.title: Disassemble with source lines interleaved
examples.explain: -S shows your C next to the instructions if built with -g.

examples.title: Summary of section headers
examples.explain: Sizes and addresses of each section.

name: nm
summary: List symbols (functions and variables) in object files, libraries and executables.
compat: Letters: T = defined in code, U = undefined (needed from elsewhere), D/B = data/bss.

examples.title: List symbols in an object file
examples.explain: Helps debug 'undefined reference': is the function defined (T) anywhere, or only used (U)?

examples.title: Show only undefined symbols
examples.explain: These must be provided by other objects or libraries at link time.

examples.title: Dynamic symbols of a shared library, demangled
examples.explain: -D reads the dynamic symbol table (what the library exports); -C makes C++ names readable.

name: ldd
summary: Show which shared libraries a program will load, and which are missing.
compat: ldd may run the program's dynamic loader: never use it on untrusted binaries; use readelf -d instead. It cannot inspect binaries for another architecture.

examples.title: List shared libraries and where they resolve
examples.explain: Each line shows a library and the path it will be loaded from.
examples.warning: Only for binaries you trust: ldd can execute code from the binary.
examples.output: 'not found' means that library is missing or not on the search path (install it, or check LD_LIBRARY_PATH / ldconfig). 'not a dynamic executable' means it is static or for another architecture.

name: strings
summary: Print readable text found inside binary files.
compat: Works on any file. Default minimum length is 4 characters.

examples.title: Find version strings in a binary or firmware blob
examples.explain: Read-only way to peek inside compiled programs, kernel modules or firmware images.
examples.output: grep exits with status 1 and prints nothing if no line matched; that is not an error in strings.

examples.title: Only longer strings, to cut noise
examples.explain: Ignores runs shorter than 8 characters, which are mostly random bytes that happen to be printable.

name: pkg-config
summary: Get the right compiler and linker flags for an installed library.

install.note: Libraries only provide .pc files in their development packages (-dev / -devel).

compat: When cross-compiling, PKG_CONFIG_SYSROOT_DIR / PKG_CONFIG_PATH must point at the target sysroot (the Yocto SDK sets these).

examples.title: Compile against a library using its flags
examples.explain: The $( ) is replaced by flags like -I/usr/include/libusb-1.0 -lusb-1.0. Leave it unquoted here so the flags split into separate words.
examples.output: 'Package <name> was not found' means the -dev/-devel package is missing or PKG_CONFIG_PATH is wrong.

examples.title: Is the library available, and which version?
examples.explain: Find the right name with pkg-config --list-all | grep -i <word>.

name: git
summary: Version control: clone, check status, view changes and history, commit.
compat: Same commands on all distributions. Large repos like the Linux kernel: --depth 1 saves time and space.

examples.title: Clone a repository (shallow)
examples.explain: Creates a new directory named after the repo with only the latest snapshot.
options: Only the latest commit, not full history

examples.title: See what changed
examples.explain: Shows the branch, modified files, staged files and untracked files. Run it often.

examples.title: Show unstaged changes line by line
examples.explain: Lines starting with - were removed, + added. git diff --staged shows what will be committed.

examples.title: Compact history
examples.explain: One line per commit: short hash and subject.

examples.title: Stage and commit
examples.explain: && runs the commit only if git add succeeded. Commits stay local until you git push.

examples.title: Discard local changes to a file
examples.explain: Resets the file to the last committed version. -- ends options so a file name starting with - is safe.
examples.warning: Uncommitted edits to <file> are lost permanently; git cannot recover them. Check git diff -- <file> first.
